A nation cannot function when its citizens inhabit entirely different realities. In the American system, anyone can publish anything to millions of people instantly, regardless of truth, motive, or consequence. This has made us uniquely vulnerable to destabilization. The difference is that corporate surveillance serves private profit. State surveillance under a clear legal framework would serve public order. It is far more democratic to have monitoring subject to government oversight and law than to leave it in the hands of unaccountable tech CEOs.

3. Consequences Are Necessary to Change Behavior

A law without a penalty is a suggestion. Currently, an individual in the U.S. can intentionally spread a dangerous lie, organize an extremist movement online, or publish classified material that damages national security, with little to no legal risk. The American ideal was that free speech would lead to truth through open competition. The internet has broken that marketplace. When speech is unlimited, the loudest, angriest, and most extreme voices win — not the most truthful. The result is a country that is ungovernable, distrustful, and constantly on the edge of internal conflict.
